::: {.callout-note title="Learning outcomes & Chapter summary"}

1. **Visualize** distributions with density plots and **explain** how they are constructed and how they differ from histograms.

2. **Select** an appropriate distribution plot based on its strengths and limitations.

3. **Create** density plots to compare a few distributions, controlling bandwidth, grouping, transparency, and count scaling.

:::

## Why bother?

In [Summaries](7_summaries.qmd),
we learned that it is important to inspect the underlying observations
to see how they are distributed,
which would be hidden if we just looked at a summary like the mean or median.
But what happens when we have too many data points
to visualize all of them individually?


::: {.callout-default .ex-prompt}

In this chart,
there are so many observation
that the plot is saturated
and it is impossible to tell
how the data points are distributed.
How do you think we could plot the observations
to more clearly see how they are distributed?

```{python}
#| echo: false
import altair as alt
import pandas as pd

# alt.datasets.data.movies().query("`Major Genre`.isin(['Comedy', 'Horror', 'Adventure', 'Drama'])").dropna(subset=['Running Time min']).to_csv('data/movies.csv')
movies = pd.read_csv('data/movies.csv')
alt.Chart(movies).mark_circle().encode(
    x='Running Time min',
    y='Major Genre',
    yOffset='jitter:Q',
).transform_calculate(
    jitter=alt.expr.random()
)
```

:::: {.callout-default .ex-hint}

We could of course increase the size of the chart
to jitter the points more,
but it would still be difficult
to get an overall idea of how the observation are distributed.
What if we could use what we learned
in the previous chapter about counting
to help us here?

::::: {.callout-default .ex-solution}

Instead of showing each individual observation,
we could visualize the counts of observations
along different intervals of the x-axis.
Conceptually, we could think of this
as first creating bins along the x-axis
(e.g. one bin could be Running Time 80-100 min)
and then counting all the observations that fall within that bin
and drawing a bar width heigh corresponding to the count of observations,
like in this animation:

![Schematic animation of creating a histogram](img/histogram-buildup.gif){#fig-hist-buildup}

:::::

::::

:::

## Histograms

To create a histogram,
we bin one axis into categorical intervals
and then count the observations withing each interval.
The reason we create intervals
is that for a quantitative variable,
there are very few observations
with **exactly** the same value,
so if we were to create
a count chart without binning,
the histogram would look spiky and sparse:

We could create the intervals manually in the dataframe
and plot a categorical count chart
as in the previous chapter
but there is a special type of chart to help us
create the bins and counts for a quantitative variable:
the histogram.

Let's create a histogram for the entire data set first,
before breaking it down into the different movie genres.

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}

### Altair

We can use the `bin()` method
on the `alt.X/alt.Y` helper classes
to automatically bin the axis
of the quantitative variable.

```{python}
#| label: runtime-histogram-alt
import altair as alt
import pandas as pd

alt.data_transformers.enable('vegafusion')
```

Vegafusion makes it easier to work with large datasets in Altair,
we must use it whenever we have a dataset with more than 5,000 rows,
and can use it as a default even for smaller datasets as well
(you can [read more about how Vegfusion work in the Altair docs](https://altair-viz.github.io/user_guide/large_datasets.html#vegafusion-data-transformer)).

```{python}
movies = pd.read_csv('data/movies.csv')
alt.Chart(movies).mark_bar().encode(
    x=alt.X('Running Time min').bin(),
    y='count()',
)
```

### ggplot

We can use `stat = 'bin'`
to automatically bin the axis
of the quantitative variable.

<!-- TODO dropna in data? -->

```{r}
#| label: runtime-histogram-gg
#| message: false
library(ggplot2)

movies <- readr::read_csv('data/movies.csv')
ggplot(movies, aes(x= `Running Time min`)) +
    geom_bar(stat = "bin", color = 'white')
```

As a shortcut for `geom_bar(stat = "bin")`,
we could use `geom_histogram()`,
which we will do from now on.
The `color = 'white'` part
creates the vertical white lines between bars;
they are optional
but tend to make the histogram more visually pleasing.

:::

Different visualization libraries use rules of varying appropriateness
to determine the number of bins.
Some prioritize adhering the bins
Regardless of which library you use,
it is a good idea to try a few different values manually
different properties of the histogram can stand out
at different bin widths,
so let's learn how to do that.

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}

### Altair

We can pass `maxbins=` to the `bin()` method
to control the number of bins.
Note `maxbins` is an upper limit on the number of bins.
Altair will create bins so that
they form easy to read intervals
(e.g. 5-10 instead of 6.3-9.4).

```{python}
#| label: runtime-histogram-bins-alt
alt.Chart(movies).mark_bar().encode(
    x=alt.X('Running Time min').bin(maxbins=30),
    y='count()',
)
```

### ggplot

We can use `stat = 'bin'`
to automatically bin the axis
of the quantitative variable.

<!-- TODO dropna in data? -->

```{r}
#| label: runtime-histogram-bins-gg
#| message: false
ggplot(movies, aes(x= `Running Time min`)) +
    geom_histogram(bins = 10, color = 'white')
```

:::

::: {.callout-default .ex-prompt}

Here we have created a few histograms for a dataset
containing finish times from the 2023 London marathon
(for male runners aged 18-39).
Explore different bin numbers for histograms
using the dropdown widget below.
Which do you think is the "right" number of bins?
And how would you explain the peaks in the distribution
that occur at higher bin numbers?

```{python}
#| echo: false
mara = pd.read_csv('/home/joel/Downloads/Respository London Marathon 18-23.csv').query('gender == 1 and agecat == "18-39"')
mara['Time (minutes)'] = pd.to_timedelta(mara['fulltime'].str.split(' ').str[0]).dt.total_seconds() / 60

min_bins = 10
max_bins = 50
bin_step = 1
bins = [20, 40, 80, 220]
bins_param = alt.param(
    name="bins_param",
    value=20,
    bind=alt.binding_select(options=bins, name='Bins: ')
)

layers = [
    alt.Chart(mara, height=200, width=500)
    .transform_filter(f"bins_param === {n}")
    .mark_bar()
    .encode(
        x=alt.X(
            "Time (minutes)",
            bin=alt.Bin(maxbins=n),
            title="Finish time (minutes)"
        ),
        y=alt.Y("count()", title="Count"),
        tooltip=alt.Tooltip('Time (minutes)').bin(maxbins=n),

    )
    for n in bins# range(min_bins, max_bins+1, bin_step)
]

alt.layer(*layers).add_params(bins_param)
```

To switch more quickly between the option,
you can use the arrow keys
after clicking the dropdown once.
You can also hover a bin with the pointer
to see the exact values for that interval.

:::: {.callout-default .ex-hint}

It seems like the peaks are
just before the round numbers 180, 210, and 240 min.
How many hours do these minute values correspond to?

::::: {.callout-default .ex-solution}

In this case,
the peaks are not a binning artefact or technical noise;
they reflect a real phenomena in the underlying data.
Many people that run races such as marathons,
set a time that they will finish faster than;
among the more popular times are even numbers
such as in this case 3, 3 h 30 min, and
4h.^[[Reference-Dependent Preferences: Evidence from Marathon Runners](https://pubsonline.informs.org/doi/abs/10.1287/mnsc.2015.2417?journalCode=mnsc)]


:::::

::::

:::

::: {.callout-warning}

### Avoid looking at just a single histogram

Various attributes of the distribution
can stand out at different bin widths.
It's therefore paramount
to look at a few different histogram bin numbers
and reflect on which features of the underlying data
they might highlight.

:::

In addition to the number of bins
impacting the shape of the histogram,
even histograms with the same number of bins
can look quite different depending on
the exact location of the bins along the x-axis.
In @fig-hist-bin-shift,
we can see that the left histogram
seem to show a long tailed distribution,
but when the bins are shifted over in the rightmost histogram,
it now looks like a potentially bimodal distribution
with two peaks.

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| label: fig-hist-bin-shift
#| fig-cap: The two histograms have the same number of bins; in other words each bin has the same width, but the start and end points of the bins are shifted slightly between the two charts.
from random import choice

cars = alt.datasets.data.cars()
bin_min = 235
bin_max = 285

mask_to_replace = cars['Displacement'].between(bin_min, bin_max)
new_values = [choice(range(bin_max, 300)) for _ in range(mask_to_replace.sum())]
cars.loc[mask_to_replace, 'Displacement'] = new_values

hist = alt.Chart(cars, height=120, width=200).mark_bar().encode(
    alt.X('Displacement').bin(),
    alt.Y('count()').title(None)
)

hist | hist.encode(
    alt.X('Displacement').bin(nice=False, extent=[35, 490]),
)
```

Because of the shortcomings of histograms

### Altair

```{python}
alt.Chart(movies, height=80).mark_bar().encode(
    x=alt.X('Running Time min').bin(maxbins=30),
    y='count()',
).facet(
    'Major Genre',
    columns=1
)
```

### ggplot

```{r}
#| fig-height: 6
ggplot(movies, aes(x= `Running Time min`)) +
   geom_histogram(color = 'white') +
   facet_wrap(vars(`Major Genre`), ncol=1)
```

:::
